title: SYSK Selects: How SPAM Works
summary: SYSK Selects rerun of an episode on SPAM, the canned pork-and-ham meat product from Hormel. The hosts open with the 2013 Carnival Splendor drift (the "Spamcation") and then cover what Spam is made of, its shelf life, and its origin: Jay Hormel's spiced ham, the New Year's party naming contest won by actor Kenneth Daigneau, and the name's unknown origin. They trace its wartime role via the Lend-Lease Act and its popularity in Hawaii and Japan (spam musubi), then describe production in Austin, Minnesota and Fremont, Nebraska, and the Spam Museum. They discuss health concerns (sodium, saturated fat, nitrites and nitrosamines, and a University of Hawaii pancreatic cancer study), Monty Python's Spam sketch, the origin of "spam" as internet term, the Waikiki Spam Jam, and a listener email about co-host dynamics.

segments.title: Opening and Carnival Splendor drift
segments.summary: Josh introduces the Selects episode on Spam. The hosts open with a story about the Carnival Splendor cruise ship losing power and drifting off Mexico, dubbed the 'Spamcation' after the US Navy dropped Spam supplies, and trade anecdotes about cruises.

segments.title: What Spam is made of and shelf life
segments.summary: Spam is described as pork shoulder and ham with salt, sugar, water, and a small amount of sodium nitrite that prevents botulism and keeps the pink color. Hormel says the shelf life is indefinite but recommends eating it within three years of the stamped date, as flavor declines.

segments.title: Origins: Hormel spiced ham and canning
segments.summary: Hormel's fresh meat business struggled, so George Hormel's son Jay Hormel moved into canned meat during the Depression. Early canning had problems because cell walls broke down and released water, and the process was refined using salt, precise temperatures and vacuum canning. Early cans used a key to open them.

segments.title: Naming contest and the name Spam
segments.summary: Hormel's New Year's Eve naming contest, where guests received free drinks for names written on slips, produced poor names until actor Kenneth Daigneau proposed Spam, reportedly for a $100 prize. The origin of the name remains uncertain, with theories such as acronyms being speculative.

segments.title: World War II, Lend-Lease and postwar popularity
segments.summary: The Lend-Lease Act let the US send food and supplies to Allied countries, and Hormel shipped large quantities of Spam, which became common in World War II rations, especially in the Pacific. Soldiers developed mixed feelings, and postwar advertising made Spam a household name.

segments.title: Spam in Hawaii, Japan and Okinawa
segments.summary: Spam is popular in Hawaii and Japan, partly due to American military presence, especially in Okinawa. Spam musubi is a slice of Spam on rice wrapped in nori, and Spam, rice and eggs appears on Hawaiian menus. Hawaii leads the US in per-capita Spam consumption.

segments.title: Production process and Spam Museum
segments.summary: Spam is made in Austin, Minnesota and Fremont, Nebraska, with a highly automated process run by about thirteen workers. Meat is trimmed, ground, mixed, piped into cans, sealed, then cooked in cookers holding up to 66,000 cans. Labels changed from lithography to plastic. The Spam Museum is free and staffed partly by retired factory workers.

segments.title: Health concerns, sodium and processed meat cancer
segments.summary: A 12 ounce can holds six servings with about 190 percent of daily sodium and high saturated fat. Light and reduced-sodium versions exist. A University of Hawaii study linked processed meat to higher pancreatic cancer risk, with the theory that nitrite forms carcinogenic nitrosamines, though the FDA has not acted. Hosts note that low-income people rely on cheap Spam.

segments.title: Cultural references, email origin and listener mail
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Monty Python's Spam sketch, Slammin' Spammy the wartime mascot, the origin of spam as internet term, the Waikiki Spam Jam, a record-eating attempt, and a listener email from Kristen in Toronto about how the hosts split speaking time. Closes with the show's contact address.
